# JavaScript for Earth Engine {#sec-javascript}

::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
Enough JavaScript to write Earth Engine scripts, and nothing more. If you already program, skim to @sec-js-pitfalls, which covers the mistakes that specifically bite in this environment.
:::

## Why JavaScript, and how little you need

Earth Engine offers two client libraries: JavaScript in the browser based Code Editor, and Python for notebooks. This book teaches JavaScript because it needs no installation, no environment management and no authentication dance. You open a URL and you are working. Appendix A covers the Python route for readers who need to integrate with an existing pipeline.

The good news is that the subset required is genuinely small. Earth Engine scripts are mostly declarations, function calls and one kind of function definition. There are no classes to write, very little control flow, and almost no data structures beyond lists and dictionaries.

## Variables

A variable is a name attached to a value. Declare it with `var`, and end every statement with a semicolon.

```javascript
var studyAreaName = 'Mahakam Delta';    // text, in single quotes
var targetYear = 2023;                  // number, no quotes
var cloudThreshold = 25;                // number
var includeRadar = true;                // boolean, no quotes
```

Names may contain letters, digits, underscores and dollar signs, and may not begin with a digit. They are case sensitive, so `aoi` and `AOI` are different variables and mixing them produces an undefined variable error.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: smart quotes
Text copied from Word, Google Docs, a PDF or a chat window often carries typographic quotes (`'` and `'`) instead of straight ones (`'`). JavaScript does not recognise them, and the resulting error message points at the wrong place. If a line looks correct and still fails, retype the quotes by hand. This is the single most common problem when readers paste code out of a document.
:::

## Lists and dictionaries

Two containers carry almost all the structured data you will write by hand.

A **list** is an ordered sequence in square brackets. Order matters, and it matters more than beginners expect: band order determines which channel is drawn red.

```javascript
var visualisationBands = ['B4', 'B3', 'B2'];        // red, green, blue
var elevationPalette = ['blue', 'green', 'brown'];  // low to high
```

A **dictionary**, also called an object, is a set of named values in curly braces. Every visualisation parameter you write is a dictionary.

```javascript
var visualisation = {
  bands: ['B4', 'B3', 'B2'],
  min: 0,
  max: 3000,
  gamma: 1.4
};
```

Two syntax rules cause most dictionary errors. Separate entries with commas, but do not put a comma after the last one. And separate the key from the value with a colon, not an equals sign.

## Functions

A function is a reusable block that takes input and returns output. In Earth Engine you write them constantly, because the standard way to process a collection is to define what should happen to one image and hand that definition to `.map()`.

```javascript
// Named function. Takes one image, returns that image with NDVI attached.
var addNdvi = function (image) {
  var ndvi = image.normalizedDifference(['B8', 'B4']).rename('NDVI');
  return image.addBands(ndvi);
};

// Use it on a single image.
var enriched = addNdvi(myImage);

// Or across a whole collection, in parallel, on the server.
var enrichedCollection = myCollection.map(addNdvi);
```

Three rules to internalise. The function must `return` something, or `.map()` receives nothing and fails with an unhelpful message. Variables declared inside a function exist only inside it. And the parameter name, `image` above, is arbitrary and local; naming it `img` or `scene` changes nothing.

## Comments

Comments are not decoration in this book, they are the teaching. Two forms exist.

```javascript
// A single line comment. Everything after the slashes is ignored.

/*
  A block comment, useful for a header that explains what a script does,
  who it is for, and what assets it expects to exist.
*/
```

A convention worth adopting: reserve block comments for section headers that describe intent, and single line comments for decisions. A comment that restates the code (`// select band 8`) adds nothing. A comment that records why band 8 was chosen over band 8A earns its place.

## Printing and the Console

`print()` sends a value to the Console tab. It accepts a label followed by the thing to print, which makes output readable when a script prints twenty times.

```javascript
print('Scenes after filtering:', filtered.size());
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: printing too much
The Console has a hard limit of 5,000 elements. Printing an entire image collection, or a feature collection of training points, will exceed it and fail. Print sizes, first elements and aggregated summaries instead:

```javascript
print('Collection size:', collection.size());   // safe
print('First image:', collection.first());      // safe
print(collection);                              // fails on large collections
```
:::

## Pitfalls specific to this environment {#sec-js-pitfalls}

Four traps catch experienced programmers, all stemming from the client and server split that @sec-paradigm introduced.

**Client values and server values do not mix freely.** A JavaScript number lives in your browser. An `ee.Number` lives on Google's servers. You can push a client value to the server, but you cannot pull a server value into a client `if` statement without an explicit and expensive `getInfo()` call.

```javascript
// Wrong. size() returns a server object; JavaScript cannot test it directly.
if (collection.size() > 0) { ... }

// Right, but slow, and blocks the browser. Use sparingly and never inside map().
if (collection.size().getInfo() > 0) { ... }

// Usually better: restructure so the test happens on the server.
var result = ee.Algorithms.If(collection.size().gt(0), doThis, doThat);
```

**String concatenation crosses the boundary badly.** Joining a client string to a server value requires `ee.String` and `.cat()`, not the `+` operator.

**Reassignment inside a loop rarely does what you expect.** If you find yourself writing a `for` loop over images, stop and read Chapter 7. There is nearly always a `.map()` formulation, and it will be dramatically faster.

**Multi line statements need care.** JavaScript inserts semicolons automatically in ways that can truncate a statement split across lines. Keep the dot at the end of the previous line, not the start of the next, when chaining:

```javascript
// Reliable
var filtered = collection
  .filterDate('2023-01-01', '2023-12-31')
  .filterBounds(aoi);
```

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Write a dictionary of visualisation parameters for a false colour composite using Sentinel-2 bands B8, B4 and B3, with a stretch you would defend over vegetation.
2. Write a function that takes an image and returns it with an NDWI band attached. Do not look at Chapter 9 first.
3. Deliberately introduce a smart quote into a working script and read the error message carefully. Recognising it once saves an hour later.
4. Print the size of a collection, then print the collection itself, and note the difference in what the Console does.
